walkthroughs.body_html:
Enzymes are biological catalysts.

They speed up chemical reactions in your body so they happen at a useful rate — at body temperature, not in a furnace.

They are proteins, made of folded chains of amino acids.

Each enzyme has a special pocket called the active site.

The substrate fits into the active site like a key fits a lock — only the right shape will do.

The enzyme then breaks the substrate apart (or joins pieces together) into the product, and the enzyme is freed to do it again.

This is the lock-and-key model.

Most enzymes end in -ase and are named after their substrate.

- Sucrose → sucrase
- Maltose → maltase
- Lactose → lactase
- Lipids → lipase
- Proteins → protease

Spot the pattern: take the substrate name, swap the ending for -ase.

mcqs.q: What kind of molecule is an enzyme?
options: A lipid
A carbohydrate
A protein
A nucleic acid

mcqs.q: Which enzyme would break down maltose?
options: Maltase
Lipase
Protease
Amylase

mcqs.q: What happens to an enzyme when it is denatured?
options: Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.
The enzyme has died because enzymes are alive.
The enzyme has been completely broken into amino acids.
Its tertiary structure (3D shape) changes, particularly the active site, so it can no longer bind substrate effectively.

mcqs.q: Why are enzymes specific to certain substrates?
options: Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.
Each enzyme can react with any substrate, but works fastest with one type.
Only substrates with complementary shape and chemistry to the active site can bind effectively.
Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.

mcqs.q: What distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?
options: Both move substances down a concentration gradient, but active transport is faster.
Active transport only happens in animals and facilitated diffusion only in plants.
Enzymes choose their substrate based on which one is most common in the cell.
Active transport requires energy (ATP) and can move substances against the concentration gradient.
